entries.title: Fatty food raises risk of colorectal cancer
entries.summary: Did you know fatty foods can increase production of an acid in your gut that promotes tumor growth? That's on top of all the other health risks linked to fatty foods, like fries and burgers.
entries.content:
August 17, 2026

Did you know fatty foods can increase production of an acid in your gut that promotes tumor growth? That's on top of all the other health risks linked to fatty foods, like fries and burgers.

The list of health risks associated with foods high in fat and low in fiber is long:

  • low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL) or "bad" cholesterol
  • clogged arteries
  • weight gain
  • heart disease
  • liver stress
  • blood sugar spikes
  • bad digestion

And the list goes on.

Now a team of German researchers has shown how so-called Western diets that are often full of fatty foods can lead to the development of one of the most common — and deadliest — cancers in adults under 50 years of age.

The researchers from the Technical University of Munich, RWTH Aachen and the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbrücke (DIfE) found that these unhealthy diets sustain certain gut bacteria that produce a secondary bile acid — which in turn promotes tumor growth.

Their results were published in the August 2026 issue of the journal Gut.

"What's special about our study is that it shows the causality," Annika Osswald, the first author of the study and a PhD student at the German Institute of Human Nutrition, told DW. "Until now, we only knew there was some sort of connection between [a certain] secondary bile acid and colorectal cancer."

How bile acid is linked to colorectal cancer

The fat in the food you eat triggers the production of primary bile acids in your liver. These acids are important ― your body needs them to break down and absorb fats. Most of the primary bile acids are reabsorbed and returned to the liver.

But a small fraction reaches the colon, where certain bacteria convert them into secondary bile acids, including one called deoxycholic acid (DCA). The more fatty foods you eat, the higher the concentration of DCA in your colon. And that's where the problems start.

Osswald and her colleagues tested this in mice in a lab. "At the core of our work to prove causality were the mouse models," Osswald explained.

The research team implanted DCA-producing bacteria into mice whose intestinal microbiome they controlled completely. Then the scientists induced colorectal cancer in these mice, and also in mice without the bacteria. The mice that had DCA-producing bacteria in their gut saw more tumor growth than the mice that didn't have it.

Cell division in the mice with DCA was increased as well. Increased cell division makes it more likely for cancer to develop, because it multiplies the chances of DNA replication errors. These DNA mutations during cell division can stack up and lead to cancer.

To see whether the process they had observed in mice also takes place in humans, the researchers analyzed stool samples from more than a thousand people, both with and without colorectal cancer. Genes of DCA-producing bacteria were found more frequently in people with colorectal cancer.

"Our results show how much a Western high-fat diet and the associated changes in the gut microbiome can affect human gut health," said microbiologist Sören Ocvirk, another author of the study.

Osswald emphasizes that the team's work is foundational, and that more research needs to be done. Still, having proven the causality between more DCA-producing gut bacteria and increased tumor growth points to possible treatments of colorectal cancer as well.

Why it's vital to better understand colorectal cancer

Colorectal cancer is the only cancer for which the mortality rate in people under 50 years has increased in the past few decades. That's according to findings published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in January 2026.

The number of deaths from brain cancer, breast cancer, leukemia and lung cancer all went down in the US from 1990 to 2023. But the number of deaths from colorectal cancer increased by 1.1% annually, starting in 2005. While the US is only one region in the world, it is often considered a sufficient indicator of such trends, especially when it comes to the Western diet.

When detected early, cancer starting in the colon or the rectum is treatable.

But symptoms frequently don't present in the early stages of the disease. And when they do, they may be misinterpreted as indications of less harmful conditions like hemorrhoids or irritable bowel syndrome.

Symptoms for colorectal cancer include:

  • blood in or on your stool
  • intermittent or constant diarrhea or constipation
  • persistent abdominal pain
  • gas or cramps
  • feeling bloated

Another obstacle to early detection is that some people may feel embarrassed discussing colorectal health symptoms with their doctor.

So, try not to be embarrassed, talk to your doctor.

How can study results help with treating colorectal cancer?

One option to be considered in the future could be microbiome transplants.

"You could transplant the microbiome of people who have fewer DCA-producing bacteria in their gut into patients with colorectal cancer," Osswald said. "That could potentially slow down tumor growth."

But the best option is to prevent colorectal cancer in the first place. While some people may have a genetic disposition to developing colorectal cancer, a lot is down to lifestyle factors.

Eating healthily, reducing the amount of meat and fatty foods in your diet, and not smoking, are some good ways to decrease your colorectal cancer risk.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: Germany news: Belgium blaze kept out of Germany for now
entries.summary: Some residents in the Eifel town of Monschau were evacuated as a massive fire in Belgium threatened to cross the border. Meanwhile, shipping shortfalls amid low river water levels could hit the construction industry.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Belgium blaze kept out of Germany for now

Published August 17, 2026last updated August 17, 2026

Some residents in the Eifel town of Monschau were evacuated as a massive fire in Belgium threatened to cross the border. Meanwhile, shipping shortfalls amid low river water levels could hit the construction industry.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A massive wildfire in Belgium has stopped its advance to the German border, firefighters say
  • Reduced cargo shipping on rivers amid low water levels could impact construction supplies, associations say

​​​​​​​Here is a roundup of top headlines from and about Germany on August 17, 2026:

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Low water levels in rivers could impact construction: industry associations

Low water levels in rivers could impact construction: industry associations

The building sector could face supply shortfalls as ships on German rivers carry less cargo because of falling water levels, construction industry associations say.

"Transport by water is becoming increasingly difficult," Thomas Reimann, the president of an association representing construction contractors in the German state of Hesse, told the DPA news agency.

He said that sand and gravel, which are often shipped in large quantities to concrete plants, are becoming harder to come by and more expensive.

The German Construction Industry Federation (HDB) also said suppliers had already warned that continued low water levels could lead to shortages in some building supplies.

Bitumen, aggregate, natural stone, fuels and mineral construction waste are among the other materials affected by the reduced shipping capacity.

HDB chief executive Tim-Oliver Müller said it was unlikely that construction would be brought to a widespread halt but that the risk of shortages, higher logistics costs and delays was growing as low water levels persist.

Skip next section Precautionary evacuations in Monschau as Belgium fire rages

Precautionary evacuations in Monschau as Belgium fire rages

Several homes in the Eifel town of Monschau were evacuated overnight as a wildfire burning in Belgium's High Fens nature reserve threatened to cross the border.

Around 30 residents from 17 homes were evacuated, with emergency accommodation set up at a nearby school.

However, by Monday morning the fire was said to have stopped its advance toward Germany amid weather conditions that are more favorable to firefighting efforts.

The fire had previously moved to within about 300 meters (984 feet) of the German border.

A spokesman for the local fire brigade said meadows between the fire and homes had been soaked with water for hours to help stop the spread of the flames.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom in Bonn wishes guten Tag to its readers at the start of a new week.

Although the recent (very) hot weather in Germany seems to be over for now, the wildfire risk remains high, as is shown by the massive blaze in neighboring Belgium.

Some streets in the border town of Monschau were evacuated late on Sunday as the flames threatened to enter German territory, but they have fortunately been successfully held back for now.

The persistent dry conditions continued to pose problems to cargo shipping on the Rhine and other rivers, with construction associations saying that supplies could be delayed and are becoming more expensive.

Read on here for more on these and other stories from Europe's largest economy.

entries.title: US actress Hayden Panettiere dies at 36
entries.summary: Hayden Panettiere's death was announced by her father in a statement to US network ABC news. The actress was known for her roles in TV shows such as "Nashville" and "Heroes."
entries.content:
August 17, 2026

Hayden Panettiere's death was announced by her father in a statement to US network ABC news. The actress was known for her roles in TV shows such as "Nashville" and "Heroes."

Hayden Panettiere, best known for her roles in US TV shows "Heroes" and "Nashville," has died aged 36, US media reports said.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen," Panettiere's father, Skip, was quoted by ABC news as saying.

The cause of Panettiere's death has not yet been announced. Her father has urged for privacy.

She would have turned 37 on Friday,

Who was Hayden Panettiere?

Panettiere began her career as a child actor, featuring in commercials and soap operas.

She gained ‌widespread recognition as the voice of Dot, the young princess ant in Pixar's 1998 animated success "A ​Bug's Life."

She earned a Grammy nomination for the film's children's spoken word album recorded a few years after its release.

Panettiere catapulted to fame with her role as Claire Bennett — a high school cheerleader ​with super powers — on NBC's television series "Heroes," which debuted in 2006 and went on to be a hit.

She also starred as up-and-coming country singer Juliette Barnes for six seasons on the musical drama "Nashville."

Panettiere also worked in two films of the satirical horror "Scream" franchise, "Bring It On: All Or Nothing," "I Love You Beth Cooper" and "Remember the Titans."

Her last appearance was in the ​psychological thriller "Sleepwalker," which released in ⁠the US in January this year.

Panettiere was vocal about her struggles

Panettiere was open about her struggles with alcohol addiction and depression.

She revealed that she had had dealt with addiction through her 20s.

Her younger brother — actor Jansen Panettiere — died in 2023 at 28 due to a heart condition.

Hayden's memoir was published earlier this year, where she spoke about her battle with mental health, the loss of her brother, and her decision to give full custody of her daughter to her former partner, Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Hundreds flee as Belgium battles wildfire at German border
entries.summary: A rapidly spreading wildfire has scorched about 2,700 hectares in the High Fens nature reserve near Belgium's border with Germany. Some homes in the German town of Monschau were evacuated overnight as a precaution.
entries.content:
Published August 16, 2026last updated August 17, 2026

A rapidly spreading wildfire has scorched about 2,700 hectares in the High Fens nature reserve near Belgium's border with Germany. Some homes in the German town of Monschau were evacuated overnight as a precaution.

Belgium is battling its largest wildfire on record which has burned around 2,700 hectares (6,700 acres) in the eastern High Fens nature reserve.

The fire approached to within 300 meters (984 feet) of the German border, causing authorities to carry out precautionary evacuations in the German town of Monschau.

Evacuations in Belgium

On Saturday, the European Union deployed three helicopters and two water bombers as Belgium deployed additional firefighters in a bid to bring the massive blaze under control.

Authorities ordered around 600 residents in parts of Waimes, Sourbrodt and Buetgenbach to evacuate as shifting winds and heavy smoke raised concerns that the fire could reach homes. Tourists were also advised to leave the area.

"You can't see a thing anymore, there's smoke everywhere," David Rodolfs, a restaurant owner in Waimes, told the AFP news agency.

A gymnasium in a neighboring municipality was opened up to offer shelter.

How have firefighting efforts fared?

The blaze, which broke out on Friday, has spread rapidly across peatlands and pine forests. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin told AFP he was "shocked" at the fire's speed and extent of the destruction.

"There is a risk that the fire could reach homes, but we are deploying all available resources to protect them," Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the regional authorities in Wallonia, said.

Difficult terrain has hampered firefighting efforts, with operations relying heavily on aerial resources and forcing firefighters to allow difficult-to-access areas to burn, according to Yernaux.

Meanwhile, Belgium activated the EU's civil protection mechanism, bringing in three helicopters and two water-bombing aircraft from the Czech Republic, Sweden and the Netherlands.

Firefighters from Germany and Luxembourg have also joined the response, while farmers have helped emergency crews by wetting down the area.

Evacuations in Germany's Monschau

Authorities in the German town of Monschau in the Eifel region, which is located just 2 kilometers from the border, told some 30 residents from 17 homes to evacuate as a precaution late on Sunday night.

However, the fire was said early on Monday to be no longer advancing toward the German border, with firefighters aided in their efforts by light rain, lower winds and high humidity.  

Monschau, a major tourist attraction in the Eifel region, has some 12,000 residents. It is particularly known for its picturesque Old Town with its half-timbered houses.

It is located just some 23 km from the site of another major blaze in Germany's Eifel region that forced some 2,000 people from their homes on Friday.

Climate change making wildfires spread faster

Belgium has experienced another spell of extreme heat, with temperatures reaching 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit) in parts of the country.

Scientists say human-caused climate change is increasing the likelihood of hot and dry conditions that allow wildfires to spread faster and burn longer.

European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib called the blaze the latest sign of the "climate upheaval" affecting the continent.

"Never before has the wildfire season started so early in the year and reached such northern latitudes," she said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton, Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: India temple stampede in Bihar kills 7
entries.summary: At least seven people were killed after a stampede broke out at a Hindu shrine in eastern India. An investigation into the incident is underway.
entries.content:
India

India temple stampede in Bihar kills 7

August 17, 2026

At least seven people were killed after a stampede broke out at a Hindu shrine in eastern India. An investigation into the incident is underway.

A stampede at a temple in eastern India's Bihar state has left at least seven people dead and over a dozen injured, Indian media reported.

The incident took place at the Ashok Dham temple in the Lakhisarai district as a swell of devotees thronged the site to offer water to Lord Shiva on what Hindus consider an auspicious Monday of the ongoing holy month of Shravan.

Shivam Kumar, a senior police officer, told news agency ANI that an electric pole fell at the site, sparking panic that led to the stampede.

"We can tell you the exact reason only after verifying everything," he added.

Lakhisarai district magistrate Shailendra Kumar told ANI that a barricade broke because of the rush and people fell on each other.

He said at least 19 people with injuries were being treated in hospital.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed his grief over the deaths in the incident.

"Pained by the loss of lives due to a stampede in Lakhisarai, Bihar. My thoughts are with the bereaved families in this hour of grief. May the injured recover at the earliest. The local administration is assisting those affected," the prime minister's office quoted him as saying.

Injured receiving treatment

A probe is underway to determine the cause of the crush.

Meanwhile, Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary said that his government had given orders for the injured to receive swift treatment.

"The news of the deaths of devotees in the accident has left my heart deeply distressed. My deepest condolences go out to the bereaved families," he wrote in a post in Hindi on X.

Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals. In March, nine people, mostly women, were killed in a stampede at another temple in Bihar's Nalanda district.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Trump says US-South Korea military drills to be scaled back
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump said annual military drills with South Korea send an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea.
entries.content:
Asia

Trump says US-South Korea military drills to be scaled back

August 17, 2026

US President Donald Trump said annual military drills with South Korea send an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea.

US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that he ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" joint military exercises with South Korea.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that the annual exercises are not only costly but "send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea, which he said has been "unthreatening and respectful" to the US.

His post comes as the US and South Korea are scheduled to begin one of their two main annual large-scale joint military exercises this week.

South Korea has been a major US ally, with their relations having endured through more than seven decades of political changes.

Trump noted that South Korea declined to help the US in denuclearizing Iran and that he has a "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

"While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, 'No thanks!'" Trump wrote.

"Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!" Trump said.

Annual drills meant to sharpen readiness against North Korean threats

The joint military exercises, called Ulchi Freedom Shield, are scheduled to run from August 17 to 27.

The drills involve 18,000 South Korean soldiers, the South Korean military told the Associated Press.

The exercises were expected to include operations to counter drones, disrupt GPS signals and defend against cyberattacks to adapt to North Korea’s evolving capabilities.

North Korea has also been aiding Russia in its war against Ukraine by providing troops.

North Korea carries out weapons test in protest to drills

Trump's announcement comes days after North Korea reportedly fired ballistic missiles toward the sea.

Pyongyang last week threatened stern steps against the US and South Korea and called the summertime drills a "war rehearsal."

North Korea routinely denounces joint military exercises between the US and South Korea as dress rehearsals for an invasion.

But it's not clear what Trump's announcement will look like since US-South Korea joint military drills were scheduled to begin on Monday.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Italy: Thieves steal key Renaissance paintings in Sicily
entries.summary: Four Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina were stolen from his Sicilian hometown on Saturday after surviving earthquakes and centuries of history. Crooks took them while locals celebrated a religious holiday.
entries.content:
August 16, 2026

Four Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina were stolen from his Sicilian hometown on Saturday after surviving earthquakes and centuries of history. Crooks took them while locals celebrated a religious holiday.

Criminals have once again targeted a small regional museum to steal priceless artworks on public display, this time in Messina, Sicily.

Local authorities say robbers bypassed alarm and security systems at the Regional Museum of Messina (MuMe), Italy, around 10:00 p.m. (2000 GMT) on Saturday evening as the city celebrated the high point of its "Ferragosto" summer holiday, the Catholic Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Thieves were able to make off with several panels painted by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina, the most important artist ever born on the island of Sicily.

Three of the five surviving panels from Antonello's 1473 "San Gregorio Polyptych" were taken in the robbery as well as a smaller, double-sided panel locked in an armored display case.

"We are devastated by what happened. They were some of Antonello da Messina's most important and best-known works. It is a tremendous loss for the museum, the city, the community and the art world," MuMe Director Marisa Mercurio told Italy's ANSA news agency.

Messina Mayor Federico Basile called the theft "deeply reprehensible," saying it was "even more painful" for having taken place as the city celebrated the Assumption of the Virgin.

The museum remained closed Sunday as investigators searched for evidence.

Works of 'enormous cultural, artistic and symbolic importance'

"It is an extremely serious and significant loss," said Mercurio, "They have stolen works of enormous cultural, artistic and symbolic importance, not only for Messina but for Sicily as a whole. All we can do now is hope they are recovered as soon as possible."

Though the sum financial loss has not been made public — initial estimates range from €70-€80 million ($81-$92 million) — Antonello's market value increased considerably in March of this year when the Italian state laid out $14.9 million (€13 million) for the purchase of another panel that he painted around 1460.

A moving two-sided panel in oil with an "Ecce Homo" portrayal of Christ (recto) and "Saint Jerome in the Desert" (verso), the purchase and news that the painting would soon return to Italy was greeted with enthusiasm.

Messina was among the cities hoping to display the newly returned work.

Antonello was born around 1430 and trained first in Naples before studying Provencal and Flemish painting and ultimately returning to Messina in 1457, where he would work until his death in 1474.

Seen as a key figure in what was an early example of technology transfer, Antonello is largely credited with bringing revolutionary new Flemish oil painting techniques to southern Europe while at the same time spreading knowledge of Italian perspective drawing among his colleagues north of the Alps.

The return of Antonello's painting to his hometown, went the argument, would have huge symbolic value for a city that lost most of its cultural heritage, including what remained of Antonello's life and work, on December 28, 1908 — when an earthquake flattened Messina and killed nearly 60% of its population in a matter of seconds.

What paintings were stolen in Sicily?

The paintings stolen on Saturday belonged to an altarpiece installed at Messina's Monastero San Gregorio until it was destroyed in the 1908 quake.

Referred to as the "San Gregorio Polyptych" in its post-quake state, it consisted of six tempera paintings on wooden panels.

The five pieces in the museum portrayed the "Annunciation of the Virgin" in two upper panels, and the larger "Madonna of the Rosary Enthroned" flanked by full-length portraits of Saints Gregory and Benedict below.

The works were the only by Antonello never to have left Messina.

Authorities say the thieves left two panels leaning against the exterior of the museum despite having removed them from the wall and gotten them outside.

Another work, the small, two-sided oil painting on wood taken from the armored case, bore the image of Christ on one side and a Franciscan monk with the Virgin and Child on the other.

What will happen to the paintings now?

Saturday's robbery comes just days after Italian authorities announced the recovery of three stolen artworks by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cezanne and Henri Matisse worth about €10 million.

Those works were stolen from a regional museum, too, the Magnani Rocca Foundation in Parma, on March 22.

Five people — allegedly Moldavan gangsters — have been detained in connection with the theft.

Despite having (often outdated) alarm systems, museums present soft targets for criminals.

Brazen thefts at museums around the world have highlighted this problem — most dramatically in Paris, where gangsters stole priceless historic jewels from the famous Louvre in broad daylight on October 19, 2025.

Experts say the fact that stolen artworks are often instantly recognizable makes them impossible to sell via reputable channels. Instead, such objects are used as collateral among crime bosses.

In Germany, members of Berlin's infamous Remmo crime family were convicted and put in prison in connection with the 2019 theft of historic jewels from the Green Vault at Dresden's Royal Palace.

Most of the jewels from the heist were recovered, albeit damaged, but the cost to taxpayers was enormous. The jewels from the Louvre heist have yet to be recovered.

Sicily's most famous art theft happened more than half a century ago, when unknown perpetrators broke into the church of the Oratorio di San Lorenzo in Palermo to cut Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio's "Nativity with Saint Francis and Saint Lawrence" from its frame and spirit it away in the dead of night, never to be seen again, after having hung there for more than three centuries.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: UAE, Saudi Arabia, others condemn Israel's rejection of Trump Gaza plan
entries.summary: The statement came as US envoy Jared Kushner and Gaza peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov held ceasefire and implementation talks with regional mediators and Hamas in Egypt.
entries.content:
Middle East

Regional powers condemn Israel's rejection of Gaza plan

August 16, 2026

The statement came as US envoy Jared Kushner and Gaza peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov held ceasefire and implementation talks with regional mediators and Hamas in Egypt.

The United Arab Emirates and seven other countries on Sunday condemned Israel's rejection of President Donald Trump's plan to end the war in the Gaza Strip.

It comes a week after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pullout will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

Trump's Board of Peace said last month that it had reached a deal for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.

The foreign ministers of the UAE, Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Egypt issued their joint statement as Trump's envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and Nickolay Mladenov, Trump's Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, were in Egypt for Gaza ceasefire-related talks.

Countries back Trump Gaza peace road map

Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough on a 15-point road map aimed at ending the war in the Gaza Strip.

The plan drawn up by his Board of Peace calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons. An international stabilization force would then work alongside a new Palestinian police force to secure Gaza.

"Rejecting the Road Map constitutes an explicit refusal to proceed with the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan, and directly threatens to derail the extensive efforts exerted by US President Trump to bring an end to the war in Gaza and establish the conditions for lasting peace," the foreign ministers said in their Sunday statement.

"Such rejection confirms that Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza and the rest of the Occupied Palestinian Territory," they added.

They called on the Board of Peace and the US "to take immediate and concrete measures within its mandate to uphold the integrity of the Comprehensive Plan and prevent any party from obstructing its implementation."

Hamas delegation joins ceasefire talks in Cairo

Kushner met Hamas chief, Khalil al-Hayya, on Sunday according to several news agencies citing unnamed sources.

Kushner and Mladenov were in Egypt and met with mediators from Egypt, Qatar and Turkey to discuss implementation of the deal.

He is due to meet Netanyahu on Monday.

Hamas on July 30 avoided using the term "disarmament," but said it would hand over its weapons to a new Palestinian governing body that would govern Gaza under the supervision of the Board of Peace.

The group, which is designated as a terrorist organization by several countries and the EU, called on mediators and the Board of Peace to "compel" Israel to approve the road map for next steps.

Netanyahu previously said Israel remained in talks with Washington despite its objections to the peace plan.

"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," said the Israeli prime minister.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Ukraine attacks Wildberries, Russia's biggest online market
entries.summary: Since mid-July, Ukraine has been targeting warehouses of Russia's largest online retailer Wildberries almost every day. Ukraine says it's disrupting front-line shipments. But experts say it's disrupting Russia's economy.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Ukraine attacks Wildberries, Russia's biggest online market

August 16, 2026

Since mid-July, Ukraine has been targeting warehouses of Russia's largest online retailer Wildberries almost every day. Ukraine says it's disrupting front-line shipments. But experts say it's disrupting Russia's economy.

Early Sunday, a fire broke out in a warehouse belonging to Russia's largest online marketplace, Wildberries, in the town of Podolsk, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Moscow. The fire was the result of a large-scale overnight attack by Ukrainian drones, most of which were intercepted by Russian air defenses.

On Friday, Ukraine struck a different Wildberries warehouse, in Tver, north of Moscow. The day before, it had set fire to another warehouse in Salavat, further east.

About 20 Wildberries logistics hubs have been under near-daily attack in the past few weeks. At least nine employees have been confirmed dead, and scores injured, while a handful of the storehouses have halted operations. 

The Moscow-based e-commerce consultancy Data Insight estimates Wildberries has lost as much as 480 billion rubles worth of goods ($5.7 billion/€4.9 billion) and about a third of its warehouse space. Combined damaged to the company and its sellers are estimated as high as 800 billion rubles ($9.5 billion).

While Kyiv argues the retailer helps supply Russia's military, Moscow maintains it serves only civilian purposes. Either way, the attacks have been placing an increased strain on Russia's economy. 

"I think [Ukraine is] going after a choke point," Fabrice Pothier, CEO of the geopolitical consultancy firm Rasmussen Global, told DW. "Wildberries is, in a way, a choke point of Russian society and the Russian economy."

Wildberries: Russia's Amazon

Wildberries is often described as Russia's answer to the Amazon marketplace.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the ensuing sanctions on Russian trade, many online e-commerce platforms such as Amazon withdrew from the region. In response, Russian authorities permitted so-called parallel imports, essentially allowing Russian companies to sidestep sanctions by importing goods without the consent of the original rights holders. 

These companies drastically undercut conventional prices, allowing their sales volume to skyrocket. In the case of Wildberries, for example, revenue increased sevenfold between 2021 and 2025. Its competitor, Ozon, offers similarly staggering numbers, with a reported $49.3 million revenue and 59% growth in 2025.

Today, Wildberries is the largest e-commerce platform in the country, controlling about half of the respective market. Ozon dominates about 30% of the market. Together, they handle goods and services equivalent to about 8.5% of the Russia's gross domestic product (GDP).

Why is Ukraine targeting warehouses?

Following the initial attacks in mid-July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy argued that the warehouses struck were "elements of Russian logistics [...] used to distribute equipment for the war: navigation systems, components for drone production, and other supplies for the Russian army."

The Kremlin has consistently rejected this claim. But an analysis by the independent outlet Verska identified "tens of thousands of military and dual-use goods" on the platform between May and August this year, amounting in sales worth hundred of millions of rubles. 

Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Zelenskyy's office, said interrupting the flow of military goods to the front lines was just one reason for attacking the company's storage space. Disrupting a business with around 6 trillion rubels in turnover, he told DW, would also affect its creditors, including Sverbank and VTB, both of which are majority state-owned.

Not only could this drain state coffers, "if [the company] were to go bankrupt, it will probably have a domino-effect on the economy," as Pothier explained.

And "there is a bigger objective at play," the consultant added, "which is to bring back war to its sender" by disrupting civilian life. As many as 400,000 sellers have been affected by the attacks, the Russian Association of Electronic Trading Platforms reported. As a result, civilians are losing sources of income, access to goods and services, and, increasingly, a sense of normality.

The platform hosts over 1 million sellers — most of them small- and medium-sized — and reaches some 80 million users each month.

But targeting Wildberries was also meant to send a message to Russian elites, according to Podolyak. These include the billionaire Suleiman Kerimov, the diplomat Anton Vaino or politician Alexey Gromov, all of whom are counted in Putin's inner circle, and possibly have varying degrees of involvement with the Wildberries company.

What makes Wildberries a target?

Wildberries has been investing in massive logistics hubs. The largest span the size of several dozen soccer fields, making them fairly easy — and highly flammable — targets.

The company is also said to have incurred substantial debt, with some questioning whether it is still able to service them. According to financial reporting of its main operating entity, RWB LLC, short-term borrowing spiked nearly eightfold between 2024 and 2025. Along with long-term liabilities, Wildberries' debt may be as high as $14 billion, with VTB as the single-largest creditor.

Now, the other state-backed creditor, Sberbank, has signaled it is preparing to absorb losses. In response to attack on Wildberries' warehouses, Chief Financial Officer Taras Skvortsov said: "Regarding [Wildberries'] credit quality, there is indeed damage. [...] Their financial condition and potential future cash flow have decreased."

Billionaire Tatyana Kim, CEO and co-founder of Wildberries, has now reportedly turned to the government for support. While the government has confirmed talks, no details on a potential decision have emerged. It is expected, however, that VTB will play a key role in rescue efforts.

This article was originally written in Russian. It was updated on August 15 to reflect the latest developments.

entries.summary: Russia says hundreds of drones targeted Moscow overnight, with six fatalities in the capital and southern Rostov region. Five people were killed in strikes across Ukraine.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine launches one of its largest attacks of war

August 16, 2026

Russia says hundreds of drones targeted Moscow overnight, with six fatalities in the capital and southern Rostov region. Five people were killed in strikes across Ukraine.

Hundreds of drones targeted the Moscow region in a sustained overnight assault that killed at least six people, according to the Russian capital's mayor, as Ukraine steps up long-range attacks deep inside Russia.

Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 600 drones had flown toward the Moscow region between Saturday evening and 6:30 a.m. local time (0330 UTC) on Sunday, adding that 201 were destroyed over the region.

What happened in Moscow drone attack?

Russia said five people had been killed in Ukraine's attacks, five in the southwestern city of Rostov and one in the Moscow region.

Sobyanin said three people were wounded in the area inside Moscow's MKAD ring road and were receiving medical treatment.

Ukraine has intensified long-range strikes inside Russia in recent weeks, targeting military and industrial facilities as well as warehouses far from the front line.

Ukraine's Kyiv Independent newspaper reported that Ukrainian forces had targeted a warehouse belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries, as well as industrial facilities in several cities across the Moscow region.

There was no immediate independent confirmation of the scale of the attack.

Where did Russia attack in Ukraine?

Russian attacks have killed at least five people and wounded dozens more across Ukraine, according to Ukrainian officials.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a missile strike on his hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed two people and injured 14 others, while another person was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.

"Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure," Zelenskyy said.

Zelenskyy said the Russian missile attack on Kryvyi Rih caused multiple casualties, with emergency services responding at the scene. The city, a major industrial center in central Ukraine, has repeatedly been targeted during the war.

In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, a man and a woman were killed when a Russian strike hit their home, regional military administration head Ivan Fedorov said.

Spanish fighter jet shoots down drone over Romania

The attack came as NATO countries on Ukraine's borders faced fresh drone incursions of their own.

Romania's Defense Ministry said a Spanish F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone early Sunday after it entered Romanian airspace from Moldova near the border with Ukraine.

The aircraft was operating on NATO duties and intercepted the drone at 5:01 a.m. local time (0201 UTC).

Debris fell in an unpopulated area of Galati county, close to the Ukrainian border.

Romanian authorities did not immediately identify the drone's origin or say who launched it.

Romania has repeatedly reported drone debris on its territory since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube.

On Friday, an Italian Eurofighter operating under NATO command also shot down a foreign drone that entered Latvian airspace.
